subject: Mathematics
title: Primes, HCF, LCM and Integers
learningOutcomes: Explain the properties of a prime number and determine whether a whole number is prime or composite.
Deconstruct a composite number into its unique product of prime factors using index notation.
Calculate the HCF and LCM of two or more numbers using both the listing and division methods.
Analyse and solve real-world word problems using HCF and LCM.
Understand negative numbers and position, compare, and order integers on a number line.
Carry out addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division on integers, fractions, and decimals.

sections.heading: Types of Numbers
sections.body: Natural numbers N are the counting numbers {1, 2, 3, …}; whole numbers W add zero {0, 1, 2, …}; integers Z include negatives {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …}; and rational numbers Q are any number written as a/b with b ≠ 0. They nest as N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q. Zero is an integer but is neither positive nor negative. Fractions can be proper, improper, mixed, or unit; final answers are usually left as mixed numbers.

sections.heading: Primes, Composites, and Divisibility
sections.body: A factor divides a number exactly with no remainder. A prime number has exactly two factors — 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, …), while a composite number has more than two. 1 and 0 are neither prime nor composite, and 2 is the only even prime. Divisibility tests (by 2, 3, 5, 7, 11) and the Sieve of Eratosthenes help find primes quickly. To test if n is prime, only test prime divisors up to √n.

sections.heading: Prime Factorization and Index Notation
sections.body: Every composite number can be written uniquely as a product of primes (the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic). Use a factor tree or repeated division by the smallest prime. Repeated factors are written with index notation: 2 × 2 × 3 = 2² × 3. Factors of a number and its prime factorization are different things — for example the factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, but its prime factorization is 2 × 3².

sections.heading: Squares, Cubes, and Roots
sections.body: A perfect square is n² (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, …); a perfect cube is n³ (0, 1, 8, 27, 64, …). A perfect square can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, or 9. Squaring and square roots are inverse operations. To find a root by prime factorization, halve every index for a square root, or divide every index by 3 for a cube root. When a number is not a perfect square or cube, estimate using the nearest one (e.g. √50 ≈ 7 because 49 = 7²).

sections.heading: Highest Common Factor and Lowest Common Multiple
sections.body: The HCF is the largest number that divides all the given numbers — take the common prime factors with the smallest index. The LCM is the smallest number that is a multiple of all of them — take every prime factor with its highest index. Both can be found by prime factorization or by the division method. For example HCF(18, 30) = 2 × 3 = 6 and LCM(30, 36) = 2² × 3² × 5 = 180.

sections.heading: HCF vs LCM in Word Problems
sections.body: Use the HCF for dividing or grouping problems — 'greatest/largest possible', 'equal groups', 'cut equally', 'share with no leftover' (e.g. the largest square tile for a floor). Use the LCM for coincidence problems — 'next time together', 'first time all occur together', 'when will they meet again' (e.g. lights flashing every 18, 30, and 40 seconds flash together after LCM = 360 seconds).

sections.heading: Negative Numbers, the Number Line, and Absolute Value
sections.body: Numbers less than 0 are negative (temperatures below 0°C, floors below ground, overdrafts). On a horizontal number line, right is greater and left is smaller, so −100 < −1 < 0 < 1 < 100 — the more negative a number, the smaller it is. Use <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare. The absolute value |n| is the distance of n from 0 and is always ≥ 0, so |−7| = |7| = 7.

sections.heading: Operations with Integers, Fractions, and Decimals
sections.body: Adding a negative is subtracting: a + (−b) = a − b; subtracting a negative is adding: a − (−b) = a + b. For multiplication and division, same signs give a positive result and different signs give a negative one. Always follow BODMAS: Brackets, then Powers/Roots, then Multiplication/Division (left to right), then Addition/Subtraction (left to right). Fractions and decimals follow the same sign rules; multiply decimals by counting decimal places, and divide by scaling both numbers to clear the decimal.

definitions.definition: A whole number with exactly two different factors: 1 and itself.
A whole number with more than two different factors.
Writing a number as a unique product of its prime factors.
Writing repeated factors as a base raised to a power, e.g. 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³.
Highest Common Factor — the largest number that divides all the given numbers exactly.
Lowest Common Multiple — the smallest number that is a multiple of all the given numbers.
Any whole number or its negative: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … (zero is neither positive nor negative).
The distance of a number from 0 on the number line, always ≥ 0; written |n|.
Order of operations: Brackets, Powers/Roots, Multiplication/Division, then Addition/Subtraction.

examTips: Remember: 1 and 0 are neither prime nor composite, and 2 is the only even prime.
To test primality, only check prime divisors up to √n — anything larger has a matching smaller factor.
HCF = common primes with the SMALLEST index; LCM = all primes with the HIGHEST index. Don't mix them up.
Keyword check: 'greatest/equal groups/share' → HCF; 'together again/coincide' → LCM.
For a square root by factorization, halve each index; for a cube root, divide each index by 3.
Master the sign rules: a − (−b) = a + b, and same signs multiply/divide to positive, different signs to negative.
